elements.id-string-12: The analysis of waiting times of electron transfers has recently become experimentally accessible owing to advances in noninvasive probes working in the short-time regime.
elements.id-string-13: We study  electron waiting times in a topological Andreev interferometer: a superconducting loop with controllable phase difference connected to a quantum spin Hall edge.
elements.id-string-14: The edge state helicity enables the transfer of electrons and holes into separate leads, with transmission controlled by the loop's phase difference $\phi$.
elements.id-string-15: In this setup, a topological phase transition with emerging Majorana bound states occurs at $\phi=\pi$.
elements.id-string-16: The waiting times for electron transfers across the junction are sensitive to the phase transition, but are uncorrelated for all $\phi$.
elements.id-string-17: By contrast, in the topological phase, the waiting times of Andreev-scattered holes show a strong correlation and the crossed (hole-electron) distributions feature a unique behavior.
elements.id-string-18: Both effects exclusively result from the presence of Majorana bound states.
elements.id-string-19: Consequently, electron waiting times could circumvent some of the challenges for detecting topological superconductivity and Majorana states beyond conductance signatures.
elements.id-string-20: Fluctuations in electron transport can greatly impact the performance of electronic circuits but, at the same time, provide us with invaluable information about the quantum-coherent behavior of conductors~\cite{Blanter2000}.
elements.id-string-21: Charge fluctuations are often analyzed by full counting statistics~\cite{Levitov1996,Bagrets2003,Bagrets2006}, which usually concerns the zero-frequency or long-time limit.
elements.id-string-22: However, experimental advances with noninvasive probes~\cite{Camus2017,Geller2019,Pekola2019} have now enabled access to the short-time regime with almost single-event resolution.
elements.id-string-23: A prominent, recently developed tool for the short-time regime is the electron waiting time distribution (WTD): the distribution of time intervals between consecutive charge transfers.
elements.id-string-24: Electron WTDs provide information about tunneling events in mesoscopic conductors, beyond average current and noise~\cite{Albert2011,Albert2012,Haack2014,Tang2014,Thomas2014,Sothman2014,Dasenbrook2015,Burset2019,Kosov2019,Kosov2021}, and have recently been measured in quantum dots connected to metallic electrodes~\cite{Gorman2017,Geller2019,Tarucha2020,Brange2021} and superconductors~\cite{Jenei2019,Ranni2021}.
elements.id-string-25: Moreover, correlations between waiting times indicate nonrenewal quantum transport~\cite{Kosov2019}, where electron transfers are not independent or identically distributed, making WTDs a source of information distinct from other statistical tools~\cite{Dasenbrook2015,Kosov2019,Kosov2021}.

elements.id-string-27: In this Letter, we analyze the potential of electron WTDs and their correlations for identifying topological superconductors hosting Majorana bound states (MBSs)~\cite{Kane2005,Fu2008,Fu2009,Qi2011}.
elements.id-string-28: There is currently an intense research activity focused on obtaining reliable signatures of MBSs, since the simplest one, a robust and quantized zero-bias conductance peak~\cite{Mourik2012,Higginbotham2015,Deng2016}, has proven insufficient~\cite{Frolov2019,Frolov2021}.
elements.id-string-29: Electron waiting times in superconducting hybrid junctions have already been proposed to detect the presence of MBSs~\cite{Chevallier2016,Mi2018,Weymann2020,Fu2022,Schulz2022} and to characterize the entanglement between the electrons forming the Cooper pairs~\cite{Rajabi2013,Albert2016,Walldorf2018}.
elements.id-string-30: These theoretical proposals extended the concept of waiting times to deal with both the spin and electron-hole degrees of freedom.
elements.id-string-31: In contrast to most approaches that include ferromagnetic leads to simplify the analysis~\cite{Chevallier2016,Weymann2020,Schulz2022}, our proposal does not involve any magnetic materials.
elements.id-string-32: Instead, we here suggest a Majorana platform that is both conceptually simple and presents important advantages for measuring waiting times of electrons and holes:

elements.id-string-137: We have analyzed the distribution of waiting times for emitted electrons and holes from a topological Andreev interferometer: a NL-SL-SR-NR junction on the quantum spin Hall edge.
elements.id-string-138: Two special features of the topological Andreev interferometer are
elements.id-string-139: (i) the emergence of MBSs when the superconducting phase difference between SL and SR is $\phi=\pi$ and
elements.id-string-140: (ii) that it acts as an electron-hole beam splitter, sending holes and electrons to different leads.

elements.id-string-376: \title{Nonlocality of Majorana bound states revealed by electron waiting times in a topological Andreev interferometer}
elements.id-string-377: We study  electron waiting times in a topological Andreev interferometer: a superconducting loop with controllable phase difference connected to a quantum spin Hall edge, where the edge state helicity enables the transfer of electrons and holes into separate leads, with transmission controlled by the loop's phase difference $\phi$.
elements.id-string-378: This setup features gapless Majorana bound states at $\phi=\pi$.
elements.id-string-379: The waiting times for electron transfers across the junction are sensitive to the presence of the gapless states, but are uncorrelated for all $\phi$.
elements.id-string-380: By contrast, at $\phi=\pi$ the waiting times of Andreev-scattered holes show a strong correlation and the crossed (hole-electron) distributions feature a unique behavior.
elements.id-string-381: Both effects exclusively result from the nonlocal properties of Majorana bound states.
elements.id-string-382: Consequently, electron waiting times and their correlations could circumvent some of the challenges for detecting topological superconductivity and Majorana states beyond conductance signatures.
elements.id-string-383: Electron WTDs provide information about tunneling events in mesoscopic conductors beyond average current and noise~\cite{Albert2011,Albert2012,Haack2014,Tang2014,Thomas2014,Sothman2014,Dasenbrook2015,Burset2019,Kosov2019,Kosov2021}, and have recently been measured in quantum dots connected to metallic electrodes~\cite{Gorman2017,Geller2019,Tarucha2020,Brange2021} and superconductors~\cite{Jenei2019,Ranni2021}.
